newsitem.title: USA: CSCE cocoa tumbles on speculative liquidation.
newsitem.headline: CSCE cocoa tumbles on speculative liquidation.

text.p: Heavy long liquidation by speculators sent CSCE cocoa futures sharply lower on Thursday, with the benchmark September contract tumbling nearly three percent to its lowest settlement in five weeks, traders said.

Benchmark September slid $42 per tonne on the day, to $1,534 -- its weakest close since June 11 -- after ranging from $1,560 to $1,526. Second-month December also fell $42, to $1,583, while the back months plunged $43.

With little in the way of fresh fundamental input, traders said the sell-off was technically driven. September breached key chart support levels, they said, activating commission house sell-stops around $1,555 and $1,545.
"There was a lot of spec liquidation and stops getting hit," said one trader. "It was like an avalanche."
Speculative liquidation pressured the market from the outset, as a weak showing in London caused the September contract to gap $16 lower at the open.
"It was due lower based on London," said another trader. "It spilled over to New York and the technicals kicked in."

Many dealers had been anticipating a sell-off by speculators, who were believed to still be net long more than 20,000 lots following cocoa's rally to nine-year highs just over three weeks ago. Since that time, the September contract has plummeted $203 -- or nearly 12 percent.

"The specs jumped-in in earnest three weeks ago and now I think they are getting tired of it," said Allendale Commodities analyst Jim Cordier. "The chart formation the last couple of days has been awful. Cocoa is desperate for some good news."

Today's downslide came despite predictions for an increase in U.S. second quarter grindings. Most analysts expected the grind, due out on Friday at 0845 EDT, to rise by five to 10 percent compared with the same year-ago period. Estimates, however, have ranged from a five percent decrease to a 15 percent increase.
"I think the (grind) numbers are getting smaller and smaller," said Cordier. "It started out a good number, but I think optimism is waning.
"I think the grind will be slightly better," he added, "but not enough to turn this market around."
In 1996, U.S. second quarter grindings rose by 4.85 percent to 82,713 tonnes against a revised 78,886 tonnes in the 1995 second quarter.
Many analysts and traders expected, however, the grind figures to have little impact on cocoa futures.
"It could be down 22 percent and have no effect on the price," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "This market is quite divorced from the fundamentals."
Spilka said the market's fundamental outlook remained supportive.

"There is going to be less cocoa at the end of the 1997/98 season due to El Nino," he said. "It is a strong El Nino and it is still building. It is already having an impact on Indonesia and Malaysia."
Technically, dealers said September's next downside target was a gap on the charts between $1,525 and $1,516. Subsequent support was seen at $1,500.
The day's volume reached an estimated 10,536 lots.
